newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian soldier can't remember shooting Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian soldier can't remember shooting Israelis.

text.p: A Jordanian soldier charged with premeditated murder of seven Israeli schoolgirls told a military court on Wednesday he had no recollection of shooting them.
Private Ahmed Daqamsa told the court he had been praying at his border post in March when he saw the girls mimicking his prayer and laughing at him.
"They were mocking me and my religion," Daqamsa told the court from his black cage in the dock. "I went to my car and picked up my rifle. After that I don't know what happened."

King Hussein said the shooting in March had shamed Jordan's army and told his troops Daqamsa should have been shot dead on the spot. But opponents of Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel have rallied to defend him.
Daqamsa was stationed in Jordan's northern border territory of Baqoura, formally returned by Israel under the peace treaty but then leased back to Israeli farmers.

He said the constant stream of Israeli tourists to the area, known in Israel as the "Island of Peace", was provocative to Jordanians. Girls dressed immorally and one group brought a dog they called Mohammad to insult Arabs, he said.
They also ignored rules banning photography in the military area. "They are not allowed to take pictures, but you know the Jews, they don't even listen to the United Nations," he said.
But Daqamsa said he had never thought of killing any of them before he shot the schoolgirls, aged between 11 and 13.
At the time of the shooting, he had been at his post for 23 hours with only one hour's break because one of his comrades had taken the previous night off to see a sick relative, he said.
Military prosecutors say Daqamsa plotted to kill Israelis for months before his attack. Prosecution witnesses have also denied that he was praying at the time of the shooting.
An army psychiatrist who checked Daqamsa this week told the court he had an "anti-social personality disorder" which could make him impulsive and do things which he knew to be wrong.
Fayrouz Sayegh said Daqamsa had an obsession with sex and twice tried to commit suicide after arguing with his mother, once by taking an overdose and another time by jumping from a high building.
But Sayegh said Daqamsa did not have any mental illness.
Daqamsa, giving evidence to the court for the first time, said he was given psychological treatment from 1991 to 1994 but stopped because he did not want people to think he was insane.
During his detention he was deprived of sleep for 48 hours, had his blanket taken away and water was poured onto the floor of his cell to stop him lying down to rest, he said.
He said interrogators had repeatedly asked him whether he had any contact with Libya, Syria, Iraq or Iran, or the militant Islamic groups Hamas and Islamic Jihad.

Interrogators threatened to put him in an electric chair for 24 hours. He said they also threatened to whip him or send him to a mental asylum if he continued to deny any political or financial motivation behind the shooting.
Daqamsa said he was made to take a lie-detector test and before one round of questioning was given an injection which made him forget what he was saying.
"I am not guilty," Daqamsa said in his final statement on Wednesday. He is due to be cross examined by prosecutors on Thursday.
